claim: EphrinB2 and EphB4 play important roles in the embryonic and early postnatal development of blood and lymphatic vessels.
source: EphrinB2 and EphB4 play important roles in the embryonicand early postnatal development of blood and lymphatic vessels (Adams et al., 1999; Gerety et al., 1999; Mäkinen et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Pdgfb-CreERT2 targets the endothelium of all blood vessels and collecting lymphatic vessels, but not lymphatic capillaries in the dermal vasculature of the ear.
source: We studied the effect on the dermal vasculature of the ear where Pdgfb-CreERT2 targets the endothelium of all blood vessels and collecting lymphatic vessels, but not lymphatic capillaries (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017

claim: Gene deletion was induced by 4-Hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) administration at 3 weeks of age, when dermal endothelial cell proliferation has stopped.
source: Gene deletion was induced by 4-Hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) administration at 3 weeks of age, when dermal endothelial cell proliferation has stopped (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing proliferation data

claim: Immunostaining of the ear skin of a 7-week-old 4-OHT-treated Ephb4flox/flox;Pdgfb-CreERT2 mouse revealed abnormal collecting vessels with ectopic expression of the lymphatic capillary marker LYVE1.
source: Immunostaining of the ear skin of a 7-week-old 4-OHT-treated Ephb4flox/flox;Pdgfb-CreERT2 mouse revealed abnormal collecting vessels with ectopic expression of the lymphatic capillary marker LYVE1 (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Ephb4flox/flox;Pdgfb-CreERT2 mice showed disruption of VE-cadherin+ cell-cell junctions in collecting vessels.
source: Immunostaining of the ear skin of a 7-week-old 4-OHT-treated Ephb4flox/flox;Pdgfb-CreERT2 mouse revealed abnormal collecting vessels with ectopic expression of the lymphatic capillary marker LYVE1 (Figure 1A) and disruption of VE-cadherin+ cell-cell junctions (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B

claim: A similar, albeit more severe phenotype was observed in the Efnb2flox/flox;Pdgfb-CreERT2 mice already 2 weeks after 4-OHT administration.
source: A similar, albeit more severe phenotype was observed in the Efnb2flox/flox;Pdgfb-CreERT2 mice already 2 weeks after 4-OHT administration (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C,D

claim: The cell-cell junctions of lymphatic capillaries not targeted by the Pdgfb-CreERT2 transgene appeared disorganized in the Efnb2 mutant mice.
source: Unexpectedly, the cell-cell junctions of lymphatic capillaries not targeted by the Pdgfb-CreERT2 transgene also appeared disorganized in the Efnb2 mutant mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting secondary effects caused by disruption of collecting vessels.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Disruption of collecting vessels causes secondary effects on lymphatic capillary junctions.
source: Unexpectedly, the cell-cell junctions of lymphatic capillaries not targeted by the Pdgfb-CreERT2 transgene also appeared disorganized in the Efnb2 mutant mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting secondary effects caused by disruption of collecting vessels.
evidence: Inferred from observation that non-targeted lymphatic capillaries show disorganization in Efnb2 mutants

claim: Gross morphology of the blood vessels and the architecture of blood endothelial junctions were unaltered in both Ephb4 and Efnb2 mutants.
source: Gross morphology of the blood vessels and the architecture of blood endothelial junctions were however unaltered in both mutants (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A-D

claim: Permeability of the skin or lung vasculature was not changed in Efnb2 mutants compared to control littermates under homeostasis.
source: In agreement with a lack of morphological alterations of the junctions, permeability of the skin or lung vasculature was not changed in Efnb2 mutants compared to control littermates under homeostasis (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Efficient depletion of EphrinB2 was shown by Western blot from total lung lysates 8 days after the first tamoxifen administration in Efnb2flox/flox;Cdh5-CreERT2 mice.
source: Efficient depletion of EphrinB2 was shown exemplarily by Western blot from total lung lysates 8 days after the first tamoxifen administration (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F

claim: No significant changes were observed in vascular permeability under homeostasis, or after VEGF- or histamine-induced vascular leakage in the lungs of Efnb2flox/flox;Cdh5-CreERT2 mutant compared to Cre-negative littermate controls.
source: However, no significant changes were observed either under homeostasis, or after VEGF- or histamine-induced vascular leakage in the lungs of Efnb2flox/flox;Cdh5-CreERT2 mutant compared to Cre-negative littermate controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Loss of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling in the postnatal vasculature leads to disruption of dermal lymphatic endothelial cell-cell junctions.
source: In summary, these results demonstrate that loss of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling in the postnatal vasculature leads to disruption of dermal lymphatic endothelial cell-cell junctions, while dermal and pulmonary blood endothelial cell junctions and barrier integrity are not altered.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: Dermal and pulmonary blood endothelial cell junctions and barrier integrity are not altered by loss of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling in the postnatal vasculature.
source: In summary, these results demonstrate that loss of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling in the postnatal vasculature leads to disruption of dermal lymphatic endothelial cell-cell junctions, while dermal and pulmonary blood endothelial cell junctions and barrier integrity are not altered.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: GFP reporter expression demonstrated efficient and specific Cre-mediated targeting of the lymphatic vasculature using Prox1-CreERT2 mice.
source: GFP reporter expression demonstrated efficient and specific Cre-mediated targeting of the lymphatic vasculature (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Efnb2 gene deletion was confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis of dermal LECs sorted from mutant and control ears.
source: Efnb2 gene deletion was confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis of dermal LECs sorted from mutant and control ears (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Loss of Efnb2 was evidenced by defective lymphatic valve formation.
source: Loss of Efnb2 was also evidenced by defective lymphatic valve formation (Figure 2A), consistent with the previously described role of EphrinB2-EphB4 signalling in this process (Mäkinen et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A and citations to prior research

claim: EphrinB2-EphB4 signalling plays a role in lymphatic valve formation.
source: Loss of Efnb2 was also evidenced by defective lymphatic valve formation (Figure 2A), consistent with the previously described role of EphrinB2-EphB4 signalling in this process (Mäkinen et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mäkinen et al., 2005 and Zhang et al., 2015

claim: Whole-mount staining for CLDN5 revealed disrupted cell-cell junctions and disintegration of the endothelial layer in Efnb2-deficient collecting lymphatic vessels.
source: Whole-mount staining for CLDN5 revealed disrupted cell-cell junctions and disintegration of the endothelial layer in Efnb2-deficient collecting lymphatic vessels (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Similar defects were observed after LEC-specific deletion of Ephb4.
source: Similar defects were observed after LEC-specific deletion of Ephb4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Ultrastructural analysis of the Efnb2 mutant ear vasculature using transmission electron microscopy confirmed disruption of cell-cell junctions, characterized by large intercellular gaps.
source: Ultrastructural analysis of the Efnb2 mutant ear vasculature using transmission electron microscopy confirmed disruption of cell-cell junctions, characterized by large intercellular gaps (Figure 2B,C)
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2B,C

claim: Efnb2 mutant vessels showed convoluted junctions with increased junction overlap compared to controls.
source: Ultrastructural analysis of the Efnb2 mutant ear vasculature using transmission electron microscopy confirmed disruption of cell-cell junctions, characterized by large intercellular gaps (Figure 2B,C) and convoluted junctions with increased junction overlap compared to controls (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2B,D

claim: Signs of cell degeneration were observed in Efnb2 mutant vessels.
source: We also observed signs of cell degeneration (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Deletion of Efnb2 in the quiescent dermal lymphatic vasculature at 8 weeks and analysis at 18 weeks of age showed junctional alterations, albeit less severe than in the juvenile mice.
source: Deletion of Efnb2 in the quiescent dermal lymphatic vasculature at 8 weeks and analysis at 18 weeks of age also showed junctional alterations, albeit less severe than in the juvenile mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Analysis of the outer lymphatic endothelial layer of the subcapsular sinus of inguinal lymph nodes showed disorganized junctions in 4-week-old Efnb2 and Ephb4 mutant mice after deletion at P12.
source: Analysis of the outer lymphatic endothelial layer of the subcapsular sinus of inguinal lymph nodes that forms during embryonic development (Bovay et al., 2018) showed disorganized junctions in 4-week-old Efnb2 and Ephb4 mutant mice after deletion at P12 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The outer lymphatic endothelial layer of the subcapsular sinus of inguinal lymph nodes forms during embryonic development.
source: Analysis of the outer lymphatic endothelial layer of the subcapsular sinus of inguinal lymph nodes that forms during embryonic development (Bovay et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bovay et al., 2018

claim: Analysis of the mesenteric vasculature of P11 Efnb2 and Ephb4 mice neonatally (P4) treated with 4-OHT showed disorganisation of lymphatic endothelial cell-cell junctions in the mutant vessels compared to controls.
source: In addition, analysis of the mesenteric vasculature of P11 Efnb2 and Ephb4 mice neonatally (P4) treated with 4-OHT showed disorganisation of lymphatic endothelial cell-cell junctions in the mutant vessels compared to Efnb2 heterozygous or Cre-negative controls (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Defective lymphatic valves and chylothorax, indicative of valve dysfunction, were observed in Efnb2 and Ephb4 mutant mice.
source: As expected, defective lymphatic valves and chylothorax, indicative of valve dysfunction (Nitschké et al., 2017), were also observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B and citation to Nitschké et al., 2017

claim: Chylothorax is indicative of valve dysfunction.
source: As expected, defective lymphatic valves and chylothorax, indicative of valve dysfunction (Nitschké et al., 2017), were also observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nitschké et al., 2017

claim: EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling regulates junctional integrity of lymphatic vessels of different vascular beds in juvenile and adult mice.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling regulates junctional integrity of lymphatic vessels of different vascular beds in juvenile and adult mice.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 2

claim: Analysis of the P11 neonatal mesenteric vasculature of the Efnb2GFP reporter mice showed that Efnb2 expression was not restricted to valves but was present in all LECs of collecting vessels.
source: Analysis of the P11 neonatal mesenteric vasculature of the Efnb2GFP reporter mice showed that Efnb2 expression was not restricted to valves but was present in all LECs of collecting vessels (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Defects in cell-cell junctions were observed in Efnb2-deficient lymphatic vessel regions both upstream and downstream of the valve.
source: In addition, defects in cell-cell junctions were observed in Efnb2-deficient lymphatic vessel regions both upstream and downstream of the valve (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Linear morphology represents mature stable junctions while reticular and jagged morphologies indicate active remodeling.
source: Linear morphology was previously described to represent mature stable junctions while reticular and jagged morphologies indicate active remodeling (Dorland and Huveneers, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dorland and Huveneers, 2017

claim: In wild type vessels, linear junctions were most frequent in both the upstream and downstream regions of the valve.
source: In wild type vessels, linear junctions were most frequent in both the upstream and downstream regions of the valve (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Discontinuous junctions were not observed in wild type vessels and were thus considered pathological.
source: Discontinuous junctions were not observed (Figure 3C), and were thus considered pathological.
evidence: Based on observation in Figure 3C and inference about pathological state

claim: Efnb2-deficient vessels showed an almost complete loss of linear junctions at the expense of an increase in discontinuous junctions in collecting vessels, both upstream and downstream of the defective valves.
source: Efnb2-deficient vessels showed an almost complete loss of linear junctions at the expense of an increase in discontinuous junctions in collecting vessels, both upstream and downstream of the defective valves (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Quantification of the morphology of LEC junctions in the lymph node capsule confirmed the abnormal high prevalence of discontinuous junctions in the Efnb2-deficient mice.
source: Quantification of the morphology of LEC junctions in the lymph node capsule (Figure 2E) confirmed the abnormal high prevalence of discontinuous junctions in the Efnb2-deficient mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Neonatal deletion of Efnb2 using the Cldn11-CreERT2 mice resulted in malformed lymphatic valves, characterized by disorganisation of PROX1high cells, in mesenteric lymphatic vessels.
source: As expected, neonatal deletion of Efnb2 using the Cldn11-CreERT2 mice resulted in malformed lymphatic valves, characterized by disorganisation of PROX1high cells, in mesenteric lymphatic vessels (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Quantification of the state of the cell junctions in regions of collecting vessels located upstream or downstream of morphologically abnormal Cre-targeted (GFP+) valve showed no alterations compared to the control.
source: However, quantification of the state of the cell junctions in regions of collecting vessels located upstream or downstream of morphologically abnormal Cre-targeted (GFP+) valve showed no alterations compared to the control (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The disruption of lymphatic endothelial cell-cell junctions in Efnb2-deficient collecting vessels is not caused secondarily by valve dysfunction.
source: These results show that the disruption of lymphatic endothelial cell-cell junctions in Efnb2-deficient collecting vessels is not caused secondarily by valve dysfunction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 3

claim: EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling has a collecting vessel LEC-autonomous function in regulating junctional integrity of lymphatic vessels.
source: Instead they suggest a collecting vessel LEC-autonomous function of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling in regulating junctional integrity of lymphatic vessels.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 3

claim: Western blot analysis of the immunoprecipitations for phospho-tyrosine (4G10) showed basal phosphorylation of EphB4, which was abolished upon EFNB2 silencing.
source: Western blot analysis of the immunoprecipitations for phospho-tyrosine (4G10) showed basal phosphorylation of EphB4, which was abolished upon EFNB2 silencing (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: EphB4 protein levels on the surface of EFNB2 silenced LECs were not compromised as stimulation with crosslinked EphrinB2-Fc could potently activate EphB4 protein.
source: EphB4 protein levels on the surface of EFNB2 silenced LECs were not however compromised as stimulation with crosslinked EphrinB2-Fc could potently activate EphB4 protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: EphrinB2 blockade induces junction remodeling and removal of junctional CLDN5 in HDLECs.
source: Staining for VE-cadherin revealed formation of thick/reticular and jagged HDLEC junctions, characterized by an increase in perpendicularly oriented VE-cadherin and junctional overlaps (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Morphological changes in junctions were observed already 3 hr after EphrinB2 inhibition.
source: These morphological changes in junctions were observed already 3 hr after EphrinB2 inhibition (Figure 4B) and became more pronounced over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Permeability to 40 kDa FITC-dextran was substantially increased in EphrinB2 inhibited compared to control HDLECs.
source: Permeability to 40 kDa FITC-dextran was substantially increased in EphrinB2 inhibited compared to control HDLECs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: While the junctional localisation of VE-cadherin was minimally affected by EphrinB2 blockade, reduction of junctional CLDN5 from VE-cadherin+ junctions was observed.
source: Notably, while the junctional localisation of VE-cadherin was minimally affected by EphrinB2 blockade, we observed reduction of junctional CLDN5 from VE-cadherin+ junctions (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D

claim: A similar phenotype was observed after siRNA-mediated silencing of EFNB2.
source: A similar phenotype was observed after siRNA-mediated silencing of EFNB2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: Depletion of VE-cadherin in HDLECs did not result in disrupted CLDN5 junctions.
source: Surprisingly, depletion of VE-cadherin in HDLECs did not result in disrupted CLDN5 junctions (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the localisation of CLDN5 at LEC junctions is independent of VE-cadherin.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: The localisation of CLDN5 at LEC junctions is independent of VE-cadherin.
source: Surprisingly, depletion of VE-cadherin in HDLECs did not result in disrupted CLDN5 junctions (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the localisation of CLDN5 at LEC junctions is independent of VE-cadherin.
evidence: Inferred from observation that CLDN5 junctions remain intact when VE-cadherin is depleted

claim: In BECs, junctional expression of CLDN5 is dependent on VE-cadherin.
source: This is in contrast to BECs where junctional expression of CLDN5 is dependent on VE-cadherin (Taddei et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taddei et al., 2008

claim: CDLN5 siRNA-treated LECs showed an increase in thick and reticular VE-cadherin+ junctions.
source: Although CDLN5 siRNA-treated LECs showed an increase in thick and reticular VE-cadherin+ junctions, monolayer permeability to 40 kDa FITC-dextran was only moderately increased (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and permeability data shown in Figure 4E,F

claim: Monolayer permeability to 40 kDa FITC-dextran was only moderately increased in CDLN5 siRNA-treated LECs.
source: Although CDLN5 siRNA-treated LECs showed an increase in thick and reticular VE-cadherin+ junctions, monolayer permeability to 40 kDa FITC-dextran was only moderately increased (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by permeability data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Depletion of VE-cadherin by CDH5 silencing resulted in a minor increase in HDLEC monolayer permeability.
source: Depletion of VE-cadherin by CDH5 silencing also resulted in a minor increase in HDLEC monolayer permeability (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by permeability data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Whole-mount immunostaining of mesenteries of P11 Cldn5 mutant mice revealed efficient depletion of CLDN5 from lymphatic junctions, with the exception of CLDN5 hot spots remaining in particular in lymphatic valves.
source: Whole-mount immunostaining of mesenteries of P11 Cldn5 mutant mice revealed efficient depletion of CLDN5 from lymphatic junctions, with the exception of CLDN5 hot spots remaining in particular in lymphatic valves (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4G

claim: Cldn5 deficient vessels showed an increase in thick and reticular VE-cadherin junctions compared to control vessels.
source: Cldn5 deficient vessels showed an increase in thick and reticular VE-cadherin junctions compared to control vessels (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4G

claim: Discontinuous junctions, characteristic of the lymphatic endothelium of EphrinB2/EphB4 mutant vessels, were not observed in Cldn5 deficient vessels.
source: However, we did not observe discontinuous junctions, characteristic of the lymphatic endothelium of EphrinB2/EphB4 mutant vessels.
evidence: Based on observation in Cldn5 mutant vessels

claim: Loss of CLDN5 did not result in obvious valve deformation or chylothorax formation at P11.
source: Loss of CLDN5 also did not result in obvious valve deformation or chylothorax formation at P11 (Figure 4G and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4G and additional observations

claim: Depletion of junctional adhesion molecule CLDN5 is not sufficient to explain the breakdown of lymphatic junctions observed upon EphrinB2 blockade in vitro or Efnb2 deletion in vivo.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that depletion of junctional adhesion molecule CLDN5 is not sufficient to explain the breakdown of lymphatic junctions observed upon EphrinB2 blockade in vitro or Efnb2 deletion in vivo.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 4

claim: In human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), blockade of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling leads to increased F-actin stress fibre formation.
source: In human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), blockade of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling leads to increased F-actin stress fibre formation (Abéngozar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abéngozar et al., 2012

claim: Stable and quiescent HDLEC junctions are aligned by thick parallel cortical actin bundles.
source: Like in HUVECs (Dorland and Huveneers, 2017), stable and quiescent HDLEC junctions are aligned by thick parallel cortical actin bundles.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dorland and Huveneers, 2017

claim: Remodeling HDLEC junctions are marked by a loss of cortical actin with concomitant increase in actin stress fibres and radial actin associated with perpendicular-oriented VE-cadherin+ junctions.
source: Remodeling HDLEC junctions are instead marked by a loss of cortical actin with concomitant increase in actin stress fibres and radial actin associated with perpendicular-oriented VE-cadherin+ junctions (Sabine et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabine et al., 2015

claim: EphrinB2 inhibition with the B11 antibody induced disruption of cortical actin as shown by phalloidin staining of HDLECs.
source: EphrinB2 inhibition with the B11 antibody induced disruption of cortical actin as shown by phalloidin staining of HDLECs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Central actin (radial actin and actin stress fibres) was increased by 61% in B11-treated compared to untreated HDLECs.
source: Central actin (radial actin and actin stress fibres) was instead increased by 61% in B11-treated compared to untreated HDLECs (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B

claim: In the blood vasculature, the tyrosine receptor kinase Tie2 (TEK) signals through the Rho family GTPases Rac1 and RhoA to organize the cytoskeleton into a junction-fortifying arrangement that enhances barrier function.
source: In the blood vasculature, the tyrosine receptor kinase Tie2 (TEK) signals through the Rho family GTPases Rac1 and RhoA to organize the cytoskeleton into a junction-fortifying arrangement that enhances barrier function (Mammoto et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mammoto et al., 2007

claim: Activation of EphB4 by crosslinked EphrinB2-Fc led to a 2-fold increase in Rac1 activity.
source: Activation of EphB4 by crosslinked EphrinB2-Fc led to a 2-fold increase in Rac1 activity (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Rac1 pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Inhibition of EphB4 activity by treatment with EFNB2 siRNA led to a 44% decrease in Rac1 activity.
source: Conversely, inhibition of EphB4 activity by treatment with EFNB2 siRNA led to a 44% decrease in Rac1 activity (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Rac1 pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Inhibition of Rac1 activity can lead to an increase in RhoA activity.
source: Inhibition of Rac1 activity can lead to an increase in RhoA activity (Wu et al., 2009b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2009b

claim: In blood ECs, spatio-temporal and antagonistic signalling of Rac1 and RhoA has been shown to regulate junctional integrity.
source: In blood ECs, spatio-temporal and antagonistic signalling of these Rho GTPases has been shown to regulate junctional integrity (van Buul et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Buul et al., 2014

claim: Junctional reduction of CLDN5 upon EphrinB2 blockade was inhibited in HDLECs pre-treated with the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632.
source: Immunostaining revealed that junctional reduction of CLDN5 upon EphrinB2 blockade was inhibited in HDLECs pre-treated with the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Cortical actin was maintained and the increase in central actin was markedly reduced in B11-treated HDLECs when ROCK activity was also inhibited.
source: Notably, cortical actin was maintained (Figure 5E) and the increase in central actin was markedly reduced in B11-treated HDLECs when ROCK activity was also inhibited (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5E,F

claim: ROCK inhibition alone did not affect the actin cytoskeleton or monolayer permeability of control HDLECs to 40 kDa FITC-dextran.
source: ROCK inhibition alone did not affect the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 5F) or monolayer permeability of control HDLECs to 40 kDa FITC-dextran (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5F,G

claim: ROCK inhibition efficiently inhibited EphrinB2 blockade-induced increase in monolayer permeability.
source: However, it efficiently inhibited EphrinB2 blockade-induced increase in monolayer permeability (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by permeability data shown in Figure 5G

claim: Continuous basal EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling has a critical homeostatic function in regulating Rac1/Rho-mediated cytoskeletal organisation and thereby CLDN5-mediated lymphatic junction barrier integrity.
source: We conclude that continuous basal EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling has a critical homeostatic function in regulating Rac1/Rho-mediated cytoskeletal organisation and thereby CLDN5-mediated lymphatic junction barrier integrity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in Figure 5

claim: Conditional gene deletion in mice revealed that EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling is dispensable for blood endothelial barrier function.
source: Conditional gene deletion in mice revealed that EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling is dispensable for blood endothelial barrier function, but required for stabilization of lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) junctions in different organs of juvenile and adult mice.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental findings

claim: EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling is required for stabilization of lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) junctions in different organs of juvenile and adult mice.
source: Conditional gene deletion in mice revealed that EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling is dispensable for blood endothelial barrier function, but required for stabilization of lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) junctions in different organs of juvenile and adult mice.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental findings

claim: Basal EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling controls junctional localisation of the tight junction protein CLDN5 in primary human LECs.
source: Studies in primary human LECs further showed that basal EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling controls junctional localisation of the tight junction protein CLDN5 and junction stability via Rac1/Rho-mediated regulation of cytoskeletal contractility.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental findings in primary human LECs

claim: Basal EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling controls junction stability via Rac1/Rho-mediated regulation of cytoskeletal contractility in primary human LECs.
source: Studies in primary human LECs further showed that basal EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling controls junctional localisation of the tight junction protein CLDN5 and junction stability via Rac1/Rho-mediated regulation of cytoskeletal contractility.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental findings in primary human LECs

claim: EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling provides a potential therapeutic target to selectively modulate lymphatic vessel permeability and function.
source: EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling therefore provides a potential therapeutic target to selectively modulate lymphatic vessel permeability and function.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on experimental findings

claim: The endothelium of blood and lymphatic vessels forms a barrier that controls the movement of fluid, molecules, ions and cells between the blood/lymph and the tissue.
source: The endothelium of blood and lymphatic vessels forms a barrier that controls the movement of fluid, molecules, ions and cells between the blood/lymph and the tissue.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge

claim: The barrier function of endothelial cells (ECs) varies among different organs and vessel types.
source: The barrier function of endothelial cells (ECs) varies among different organs and vessel types.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge

claim: The blood brain barrier (BBB) is formed of a continuous layer of ECs connected by specialized tight junctions and adherens junctions.
source: The blood brain barrier (BBB), for example, is formed of a continuous layer of ECs connected by specialized tight junctions and adherens junctions (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2015

claim: Blood vessels of the kidney and small intestine are lined by fenestrated ECs to facilitate rapid exchange, uptake and secretion of fluids, solutes and molecules.
source: In contrast, blood vessels of the kidney and small intestine are lined by fenestrated ECs to facilitate rapid exchange, uptake and secretion of fluids, solutes and molecules (Aird, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aird, 2012

claim: The architecture of lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) junctions differs between the different vessel types.
source: The architecture of lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) junctions also differs between the different vessel types (Baluk et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baluk et al., 2007

claim: Highly permeable button-like junctions of lymphatic capillaries allow uptake of fluid from the interstitium.
source: Highly permeable button-like junctions of lymphatic capillaries allow uptake of fluid from the interstitium.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge

claim: Collecting lymphatic vessels are equipped with continuous zipper-like junctions preventing excessive leakage.
source: The lymph is then drained and transported via collecting lymphatic vessels that are equipped with continuous zipper-like junctions preventing excessive leakage (Baluk et al., 2007; Potente and Mäkinen, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baluk et al., 2007 and Potente and Mäkinen, 2017

claim: The molecular mechanisms that establish and maintain functionally specialised junctional features of different vessel types are poorly understood.
source: The molecular mechanisms that establish and maintain such functionally specialised junctional features of different vessel types are poorly understood.
evidence: Statement about current state of scientific knowledge

claim: Vascular integrity is regulated by junctional adhesion molecules, of which the adherens junction molecule vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin and the tight junction molecule Claudin 5 (CLDN5) have received particular attention.
source: Vascular integrity is regulated by junctional adhesion molecules, of which the adherens junction molecule vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin and the tight junction molecule Claudin 5 (CLDN5) have received particular attention.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge

claim: Dysregulation of VE-cadherin can result in junctional disruption, increased vessel permeability and severe (lymph)edema formation.
source: Dysregulation of VE-cadherin can result in junctional disruption, increased vessel permeability and severe (lymph)edema formation (Frye et al., 2015; Hägerling et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frye et al., 2015; Hägerling et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019

claim: Endothelial loss of VE-cadherin in adult mice results in junctional disruption and increased vascular permeability in the heart and lung, but not the skin and brain.
source: For example, endothelial loss of VE-cadherin in adult mice results in junctional disruption and increased vascular permeability in the heart and lung, but not the skin and brain (Frye et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frye et al., 2015

claim: LEC-specific deletion of VE-cadherin in adult mice leads to organ-specific disruption of endothelial junctions affecting the mesenteric collecting vessels but not dermal lymphatic vessels.
source: LEC-specific deletion of VE-cadherin in adult mice similarly leads to organ-specific disruption of endothelial junctions affecting the mesenteric collecting vessels but not dermal lymphatic vessels (Hägerling et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hägerling et al., 2018 and Yang et al., 2019

claim: CLDN5 is absent from certain phenotypically 'leaky' vessels.
source: Unlike VE-cadherin expressed in all ECs, CLDN5 is absent from certain phenotypically 'leaky' vessels (Benz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Benz et al., 2019

claim: In the skin, CLDN5 is not expressed in blood vessels that are permissive to VEGF-induced vascular leakage.
source: For instance, in the skin, CLDN5 is not expressed in blood vessels that are permissive to VEGF-induced vascular leakage (Honkura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Honkura et al., 2018

claim: CLDN5 is critical for the establishment and maintenance of the BBB.
source: In line with a function in junctional stabilization, CLDN5 is critical for the establishment and maintenance of the BBB (Greene et al., 2018; Nitta et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greene et al., 2018 and Nitta et al., 2003

claim: CLDN5 is highly expressed in the phenotypically 'permeable' lymphatic endothelium including lymphatic capillaries.
source: CLDN5 is however highly expressed in the phenotypically 'permeable' lymphatic endothelium including lymphatic capillaries (Baluk et al., 2007), where its function is not known.
evidence: Supported by citation to Baluk et al., 2007

claim: The function of CLDN5 in lymphatic capillaries is not known.
source: CLDN5 is however highly expressed in the phenotypically 'permeable' lymphatic endothelium including lymphatic capillaries (Baluk et al., 2007), where its function is not known.
evidence: Statement about current state of scientific knowledge

claim: The junctional adhesion molecules are intracellularly associated to the actin cytoskeleton.
source: The junctional adhesion molecules are intracellularly associated to the actin cytoskeleton (Dejana et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dejana et al., 2009

claim: The molecular control of endothelial cytoskeletal dynamics presents a second important leverage point that regulates vascular integrity.
source: The molecular control of endothelial cytoskeletal dynamics presents therefore a second important leverage point that regulates vascular integrity.

claim: Quiescent endothelia are characterized by a balance of actin stabilization and myosin-based actin pulling forces that are constantly applied to endothelial junctions.
source: Quiescent endothelia are characterized by a balance of actin stabilization and myosin-based actin pulling forces that are constantly applied to endothelial junctions.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge

claim: Elevation of myosin-based actin contractility activates endothelial junctions.
source: Elevation of myosin-based actin contractility activates endothelial junctions.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge

claim: Rho GTPases are key regulators of cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: Rho GTPases are key regulators of such cytoskeletal dynamics (Dorland and Huveneers, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dorland and Huveneers, 2017

claim: Differential expression and function of Rho GTPase regulators, such as the guanosine nucleotide exchange factor Vav3, has been proposed to contribute to barrier diversity across different blood vessels.
source: Differential expression and function of Rho GTPase regulators, such as the guanosine nucleotide exchange factor Vav3, has been proposed to contribute to barrier diversity across different blood vessels (Hilfenhaus et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hilfenhaus et al., 2018

claim: Upstream regulators of Rho GTPases may provide another level for organ- and vessel-type specific barrier regulation.
source: Upstream regulators of Rho GTPases may provide another level for organ- and vessel-type specific barrier regulation.
evidence: Speculative statement based on scientific reasoning

claim: EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling is a critical and selective regulator of collecting lymphatic vessel integrity.
source: Here, we identified EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling as a critical and selective regulator of collecting lymphatic vessel integrity.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding

claim: Inducible EC-specific deletion of Efnb2 or Ephb4 disrupted lymphatic endothelial junctions in several organs while dermal and pulmonary blood vessel barrier function was not compromised.
source: Inducible EC-specific deletion of Efnb2 or Ephb4 disrupted lymphatic endothelial junctions in several organs while dermal and pulmonary blood vessel barrier function was not compromised.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding

claim: Inhibition of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling led to reduction in junctional CLDN5 while VE-cadherin was not affected in primary human LECs.
source: Studies in primary human LECs further showed that inhibition of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling led to reduction in junctional CLDN5 while VE-cadherin was not affected.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding

claim: LEC-specific deletion of Cldn5 in postnatal mice did not fully recapitulate the junctional phenotype observed in Efnb2/Ephb4-deficient vessels.
source: LEC-specific deletion of Cldn5 in postnatal mice did not however fully recapitulate the junctional phenotype observed in Efnb2/Ephb4-deficient vessels.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding

claim: Basal EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling regulates junctional localisation of CLDN5 and junction stability via Rac1/Rho-mediated control of cytoskeletal contractility in primary LECs.
source: Interestingly, we found that basal EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling regulates junctional localisation of CLDN5 and junction stability via Rac1/Rho-mediated control of cytoskeletal contractility in primary LECs.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding

claim: EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling provides a potential therapeutic target for intervention of diseases associated with abnormal lymphatic vessel permeability.
source: Our results suggest that EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling provides a potential therapeutic target for intervention of diseases associated with abnormal lymphatic vessel permeability.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on experimental findings

claim: Fluid uptake by lymphatic capillaries is a critical attribute of the lymphatic vasculature.
source: Although fluid uptake by lymphatic capillaries is a critical attribute of the lymphatic vasculature, the barrier function of collecting lymphatic vessels is also important by ensuring efficient fluid drainage as well as lymph node delivery of antigens and immune cells.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge

claim: The barrier function of collecting lymphatic vessels is important by ensuring efficient fluid drainage as well as lymph node delivery of antigens and immune cells.
source: Although fluid uptake by lymphatic capillaries is a critical attribute of the lymphatic vasculature, the barrier function of collecting lymphatic vessels is also important by ensuring efficient fluid drainage as well as lymph node delivery of antigens and immune cells.
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge

claim: EphrinB2 and EphB4 are critical homeostatic regulators of collecting lymphatic vessel integrity.
source: Here, we identified the transmembrane ligand EphrinB2 and its receptor EphB4 as critical homeostatic regulators of collecting lymphatic vessel integrity.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding from the abstract

claim: Postnatal deletion of Efnb2 or Ephb4 in endothelial cells using the Pdgfb-CreERT2 or Cdh5-CreERT2 selectively disrupted the integrity of collecting lymphatic vessels in multiple organs.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that postnatal deletion of Efnb2 or Ephb4 in endothelial cells using the Pdgfb-CreERT2 or Cdh5-CreERT2 selectively disrupted the integrity of collecting lymphatic vessels in multiple organs, but did not compromise the barrier function of dermal and pulmonary blood vessels.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding from the Discussion

claim: The different requirements of BECs and LECs for junctional stability may be related to different dependencies on cell-cell vs. cell-matrix adhesions and substrate stiffness.
source: The different requirements of BECs and LECs for junctional stability may be related to different dependencies on cell-cell vs. cell-matrix adhesions and substrate stiffness.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed differences

claim: Collecting lymphatic vessels lack an elastic lamina, have a thinner basement membrane and less mural cell support compared to arteries and veins.
source: In contrast to arteries and veins, collecting lymphatic vessels lack an elastic lamina, have a thinner basement membrane and less mural cell support (Potente and Mäkinen, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Potente and Mäkinen, 2017

claim: Collecting vessel LECs may experience a less rigid extracellular matrix (ECM), which has been associated with an increase in cell-cell coupling in favour of cell-ECM adhesions that are strengthened on stiffer matrix.
source: Collecting vessel LECs may thus experience a less rigid extracellular matrix (ECM), which has been associated with an increase in cell-cell coupling in favour of cell-ECM adhesions that are strengthened on stiffer matrix (Polio et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citation to Polio et al., 2019

claim: Efnb2 is upregulated in LECs grown on soft in comparison to stiff matrices.
source: Although this hypothesis would need to be tested experimentally, it is interesting to note that Efnb2 is upregulated in LECs grown on soft in comparison to stiff matrices (Frye et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frye et al., 2018

claim: Blood endothelial progenitors showed an increase in expression of the arterial marker EphrinB2 cultured on stiff (arterial) matrices.
source: However, blood endothelial progenitors showed an increase in expression of the arterial marker EphrinB2 cultured on stiff (arterial) matrices (Xue et al., 2017), suggesting that upregulation of Efnb2 on soft matrices is an LEC-specific phenomenon.
evidence: Supported by citation to Xue et al., 2017

claim: Upregulation of Efnb2 on soft matrices is an LEC-specific phenomenon.
source: However, blood endothelial progenitors showed an increase in expression of the arterial marker EphrinB2 cultured on stiff (arterial) matrices (Xue et al., 2017), suggesting that upregulation of Efnb2 on soft matrices is an LEC-specific phenomenon.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of LEC and BEC behavior on different matrices

claim: The phenotype appeared stronger and developed more rapidly upon Efnb2 deletion compared to Ephb4 deletion.
source: Although disruption of LEC junctions was observed in both Efnb2 and Ephb4 deficient vessels, the phenotype appeared stronger and developed more rapidly upon Efnb2 deletion.
evidence: Observation from experimental data

claim: EphrinB2 reverse signalling may play a role in LEC junction regulation.
source: It is possible that EphrinB2 reverse signalling plays a role and accounts for this difference.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed difference

claim: Genetic deletion of the PDZ binding domain of EphrinB2 led to defects in developmental lymphatic vessel remodeling and collecting vessel maturation.
source: Our previous work showed that genetic deletion of the PDZ binding domain of EphrinB2 led to defects in developmental lymphatic vessel remodeling and collecting vessel maturation (Mäkinen et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mäkinen et al., 2005

claim: The PDZ mutation affects not only the ligand-mediated reverse but also dampens receptor-mediated forward signalling.
source: Although this suggested a role for EphrinB2 reverse signalling, it was later shown that the PDZ mutation affects not only the ligand-mediated reverse but also dampens receptor-mediated forward signalling (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015

claim: Forward signalling through the EphB4 receptor is the main Ephrin signalling pathway for collecting vessel and valve development.
source: Genetic deletion and antibody-mediated inhibition of EphB4 further established the forward signalling through the receptor as being the main Ephrin signalling pathway for collecting vessel and valve development (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015

claim: The basal EphrinB2-dependent phosphorylation of EphB4 observed in LECs supports forward signalling through the receptor.
source: The basal EphrinB2-dependent phosphorylation of EphB4 we observed in LECs supports, although does not prove this notion.
evidence: Inference from experimental observation

claim: Faster depletion of EphrinB2 upon genetic deletion could explain the rapid development of a severe phenotype.
source: It is also possible that the turnover of EphrinB2 and EphB4 proteins is different, such that faster depletion of EphrinB2 upon genetic deletion could explain the rapid development of a severe phenotype.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed difference

claim: A role for EphB4 in maintaining vascular integrity in the heart was recently demonstrated.
source: Although we did not observe blood vessel defects in the skin and lung of Efnb2 or Ephb4 deleted mice, a role for EphB4 in maintaining vascular integrity in the heart was recently demonstrated (Luxán et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luxán et al., 2019

claim: Endothelial-specific deletion of Ephb4 in blood vessels in adult mice resulted in a hypertrophic cardiac phenotype that was attributed to a dysfunctional caveolae-mediated recycling of focal adhesion and junctional molecules specifically in coronary capillaries but not in skeletal muscle capillaries.
source: Endothelial-specific deletion of Ephb4 in blood vessels in adult mice resulted in a hypertrophic cardiac phenotype that was attributed to a dysfunctional caveolae-mediated recycling of focal adhesion and junctional molecules specifically in coronary capillaries but not in skeletal muscle capillaries (Luxán et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luxán et al., 2019

claim: Organ-specific differences exist in the susceptibility to disruption of vascular integrity due to differences in the magnitude of mechanical stress they constantly have to resist.
source: It has been suggested that organ-specific differences exist in the susceptibility to disruption of vascular integrity due to differences in the magnitude of mechanical stress they constantly have to resist (Frye et al., 2015; Hägerling et al., 2018; Luxán et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frye et al., 2015; Hägerling et al., 2018; Luxán et al., 2019

claim: Junctional alterations may occur at a later time-point in Efnb2/Ephb4-deficient dermal or pulmonary blood vessels and/or in context of specific pathological conditions.
source: It is therefore possible that junctional alterations occur at a later time-point in Efnb2/Ephb4-deficient dermal or pulmonary blood vessels and/or in context of specific pathological conditions.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential future observations

claim: LEC-specific deletion of Efnb2 or Ephb4 using the Prox1-CreERT2 mice led to global disruption of junctional integrity of collecting lymphatic vessels in all tissues analysed (skin, mesentery and lymph node).
source: However, it is also interesting to note that LEC-specific deletion of Efnb2 or Ephb4 using the Prox1-CreERT2 mice led to global disruption of junctional integrity of collecting lymphatic vessels in all tissues analysed (skin, mesentery and lymph node), suggesting a general role of this pathway in LEC junction maintenance.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling has a general role in LEC junction maintenance.
source: However, it is also interesting to note that LEC-specific deletion of Efnb2 or Ephb4 using the Prox1-CreERT2 mice led to global disruption of junctional integrity of collecting lymphatic vessels in all tissues analysed (skin, mesentery and lymph node), suggesting a general role of this pathway in LEC junction maintenance.
evidence: Inferred from observation of consistent phenotype across multiple tissues

claim: Fluid shear stress (FSS) has been extensively described to regulate endothelial junctions and lymphatic valve morphogenesis.
source: ECs are subjected to fluid shear stress (FSS) due to the friction between the ECs and the blood or lymph. FSS has been extensively described to regulate endothelial junctions and lymphatic valve morphogenesis Gordon et al., 2020.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2020

claim: Loss of EphrinB2-EphB4 signalling resulted in lymphatic valve defects.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Mäkinen et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2015), we found that loss of EphrinB2-EphB4 signalling resulted in lymphatic valve defects.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Mäkinen et al., 2005 and Zhang et al., 2015

claim: Genetic inactivation of the mechanosensitive transcription factor Foxc2 results in degeneration of lymphatic valves and disruption of LEC junctions.
source: Interestingly, genetic inactivation of the mechanosensitive transcription factor Foxc2 also results in degeneration of lymphatic valves and disruption of LEC junctions (Sabine et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabine et al., 2015

claim: The junctional phenotype in the Foxc2-deficient vessels is restricted to the valve sinus, where flow recirculation maintains high FOXC2 expression.
source: The junctional phenotype in the Foxc2-deficient vessels is however restricted to the valve sinus, where flow recirculation maintains high FOXC2 expression (Sabine et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabine et al., 2015

claim: Lymphatic capillaries express Efnb2.
source: Lymphatic capillaries also express Efnb2 (Bazigou et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bazigou et al., 2011

claim: The authors were not able to assess the potential cell-autonomous role of EphrinB2 in the formation and maintenance of button junctions in lymphatic capillaries because they were affected secondary to deletion of Efnb2 in collecting vessels.
source: However, we were not able to assess the potential cell-autonomous role of EphrinB2 in the formation and maintenance of button junctions in lymphatic capillaries because they were affected secondary to deletion of Efnb2 in collecting vessels.
evidence: Statement about limitation of the study

claim: LEC-specific deletion of VE-cadherin resulted in junctional defects in and fragmentation of lacteal lymphatic capillaries in the intestinal villi secondary to defects in the mesenteric collecting lymphatic vessels.
source: Interestingly, LEC-specific deletion of VE-cadherin was previously shown to result in junctional defects in and fragmentation of lacteal lymphatic capillaries in the intestinal villi secondary to defects in the mesenteric collecting lymphatic vessels (Hägerling et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hägerling et al., 2018

claim: Normal function of collecting vessels, ensuring efficient lymph flow, is critical for the maintenance of LEC junctions in lymphatic capillaries.
source: These observations suggests that normal function of collecting vessels, ensuring efficient lymph flow, is critical for the maintenance of LEC junctions in lymphatic capillaries.
evidence: Inferred from observations of secondary effects on capillaries when collecting vessels are disrupted

claim: VE-cadherin-mediated adherens junctions have important roles in the development and maintenance of lymphatic vessels.
source: ECs are interconnected via VE-cadherin-mediated adherens junctions that have important roles in the development and maintenance of lymphatic vessels (Dartsch et al., 2014; Hägerling et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dartsch et al., 2014; Hägerling et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019

claim: The phenotype in both vascular beds (dermal and mesenteric) observed upon loss of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling suggests the involvement of VE-cadherin-independent mechanisms of junction disruption.
source: This is different from the phenotype in both vascular beds observed upon loss of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling, which suggests the involvement of VE-cadherin-independent mechanisms of junction disruption.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes

claim: The role of other molecular players besides VE-cadherin was supported by lack of effect of EphrinB2/EphB4 inhibition on VE-cadherin localisation or levels in HDLECs in vitro.
source: The role of other molecular players was further supported by lack of effect of EphrinB2/EphB4 inhibition on VE-cadherin localisation or levels in HDLECs in vitro.
evidence: Based on experimental observations in HDLECs

claim: EphrinB2/EphB4 blockade resulted in reduction in the junctional localisation of CLDN5.
source: Instead, we found that EphrinB2/EphB4 blockade resulted in reduction in the junctional localisation of CLDN5.
evidence: Based on experimental observations in HDLECs

claim: CLDN5 has a more prominent role in controlling LEC junction integrity compared to VE-cadherin.
source: Although our data suggest a more prominent role of CLDN5 in controlling LEC junction integrity compared to VE-cadherin, cross-talk and compensation between CLDN5 and VE-cadherin is likely to occur.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations

claim: Cross-talk and compensation between CLDN5 and VE-cadherin is likely to occur.
source: Although our data suggest a more prominent role of CLDN5 in controlling LEC junction integrity compared to VE-cadherin, cross-talk and compensation between CLDN5 and VE-cadherin is likely to occur.
evidence: Speculative statement based on scientific reasoning

claim: Elevation of myosin-based actin contractility activates endothelial junctions, but abnormally increased contractility can ultimately lead to adherens junction disruption and loss of vascular integrity.
source: Elevation of myosin-based actin contractility activates endothelial junctions, but abnormally increased contractility can ultimately lead to adherens junction disruption and loss of vascular integrity (Faurobert et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Faurobert et al., 2013

claim: Loss of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling in primary LECs led to an increase in actin stress fibres that was attributed to increased Rho activity.
source: In agreement with previous findings in HUVECs (Abéngozar et al., 2012), we found that loss of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling in primary LECs led to an increase in actin stress fibres that was attributed to increased Rho activity.
evidence: Based on experimental observations and citation to Abéngozar et al., 2012

claim: Continuous basal activation of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling provides a homeostatic control of Rac1/Rho-mediated cytoskeletal contractility to regulate LEC junction integrity.
source: Although in vivo validation remains to be done, our findings support a concept that continuous basal activation of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling provides a homeostatic control of Rac1/Rho-mediated cytoskeletal contractility to regulate LEC junction integrity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings with acknowledgment of need for in vivo validation

claim: Loss of (valve-specific) FOXC2 and FOXC1 in LECs resulted in increased actin stress fibre formation and Rho activity.
source: Interestingly, loss of (valve-specific) FOXC2 and FOXC1 in LECs was recently shown to result in increased actin stress fibre formation and Rho activity, suggesting similar mechanisms of junctional regulation in valve LECs (Norden et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Norden et al., 2020

claim: Similar mechanisms of junctional regulation exist in valve LECs.
source: Interestingly, loss of (valve-specific) FOXC2 and FOXC1 in LECs was recently shown to result in increased actin stress fibre formation and Rho activity, suggesting similar mechanisms of junctional regulation in valve LECs (Norden et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes

claim: Ablation of the adhesion molecule CLDN5 was not sufficient to induce a breakdown of LEC junctions in the absence of activation of the cytoskeleton.
source: It may therefore not be surprising that ablation of the adhesion molecule CLDN5 was not sufficient to induce a breakdown of LEC junctions in the absence of activation of the cytoskeleton.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings

claim: In established blood vessels, basal Tie2 receptor signalling mediates stabilization of pulmonary endothelial junctions via the actin cytoskeleton even in the absence of VE-cadherin.
source: A similar concept has been suggested in established blood vessels, whereby basal Tie2 receptor signalling mediates stabilization of pulmonary endothelial junctions via the actin cytoskeleton even in the absence of VE-cadherin (Frye et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frye et al., 2015

claim: Continuous basal activation of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling provides a critical homeostatic mechanism regulating Rac1/Rho-mediated cytoskeletal contractility in LECs and integrity of cell junctions in collecting lymphatic vessels in vivo.
source: In conclusion, we show that continuous basal activation of EphrinB2/EphB4 signalling provides a critical homeostatic mechanism regulating Rac1/Rho-mediated cytoskeletal contractility in LECs and integrity of cell junctions in collecting lymphatic vessels in vivo.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all experimental findings

claim: Activation of the EphB4 receptor or downstream signalling components may provide an opportunity to overcome pathological hyperpermeability and restore basal permeability of collecting lymphatic vessels.
source: Activation of the EphB4 receptor or downstream signalling components may thus provide an opportunity to overcome pathological hyperpermeability and restore basal permeability of collecting lymphatic vessels, thereby presenting a potential strategy for selective modulation of lymphatic vessel function.
evidence: Speculative therapeutic implication based on experimental findings

claim: Activation of the EphB4 receptor or downstream signalling components presents a potential strategy for selective modulation of lymphatic vessel function.
source: Activation of the EphB4 receptor or downstream signalling components may thus provide an opportunity to overcome pathological hyperpermeability and restore basal permeability of collecting lymphatic vessels, thereby presenting a potential strategy for selective modulation of lymphatic vessel function.
